title: Delta SKU fingerprint and noise characterization
content:
Context:
This is an exploratory notebook-style writeup capturing a set of microbenchmarks and noisy-probe experiments we ran to surface small but production-relevant differences across cloud GPU SKUs (A100/H100/L40S) and driver/CUDA permutations. The goal was not a comprehensive performance matrix but to identify reproducible fingerprints (systematic deltas) and noise modes that correlate with driver or SKU variables so the runtime can route or adapt safely.

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- We observed two classes of reproducible deltas: deterministic throughput/efficiency differences (expected from architecture/FP16 kernels) and non-deterministic tail events (jitter) correlated with driver+cuda combos and host kernel versions.
- H100 showed best steady-state effective decoding throughput on long contexts (>8k) for our compiled kernels, but under a specific NVIDIA driver (535.x) with CUDA 12.2 we saw p99 spikes that disappeared when downgrading to driver 525.x.
- L40S presents a consistent moderate-power thermal ramp under sustained heavy prefill+decode workloads leading to throughput drift after ~45 minutes; this is amplified in regions where the cloud provider underprovisions host CPU interrupts.
- A100 variants are the least noisy across all drivers we tested, but show larger allocation fragmentation when using large KV-cache pooling strategies on smaller-memory SKUs (40GB vs 80GB).
- Recommendation: add a simple driver+cuda fingerprint check during node admission (runtime probe kernel) and an adaptive fallback policy: if tail-jitter > threshold, route to alternative driver-compatible SKUs or enforce isolated allocation.

Experimental setup (short):
- Models used: distilled-7B-like prefill (2k prompt) + autoreg decode (max 512) and a 16k long-context transformer prefill + 2k decode (to stress KV cache).
- Runtimes: our production compiled runtime (v3.7.1-experimental) with identical kernel selection heuristics.
- SKUs: NVidia A100 80GB (cloud sku family a100-v5), H100 80GB (h100-v1), L40S 48GB (l40s-v1). Also small-memory A100 40GB instance to reproduce fragmentation.
- Drivers/CUDA tested: driver 525.85 + CUDA 11.8; driver 535.104 + CUDA 12.2; driver 470.x + CUDA 11.4 (legacy).
- Workload patterns: steady small-batch decode (batch=1, interarrival 10-30ms), medium batch pack (batch=8), long-prefill heavy KV churn (simulated many distinct contexts).
- Measurement: token throughput, p50/p90/p95/p99 per-token latency, power draw (when available), host CPU steal/interrupt rates, GPU SM utilization, kernel launch rate, and allocation failure/retry counts.

Key observations and examples:
1) Driver-linked tail amplification (H100 + driver 535.x):
   - Under long-context prefill+decode, p99 per-token latency on H100+535.x spiked up to 3.6x baseline intermittently (short bursts lasting 200–800ms) while p50 remained stable. Lowering driver to 525.x eliminated the p99 bursts almost entirely.
   - eBPF traces show correlated kernel launch serialization around times of NVLink peer-sync (we hypothesize a driver runtime serialization/regression).
   - Action: runtime should measure a short bursty decode probe during node join; if p99/p50 ratio > 4, mark node as "tail-sensitive".

2) L40S thermal and host-CPU coupling:
   - Long sustained KV churn (many large prefill requests) produced steady power increase; after ~45 minutes the effective token throughput decreased by ~12% on L40S compared to the first 10 minutes.
   - Cloud-hosted instances where host CPU steal > 5% exacerbate this (we think interrupt handling and PCIe DMA servicing patterns matter).
   - Experiment note: adding a tiny CPU affinity pinning and isolcpus on test instances reduced the drift by ~6 percentage points.

3) A100 fragmentation with large KV pools:
   - On A100 40GB with aggressive KV caching across mixed-length contexts we saw allocation failures and eviction churn that reduced useful throughput by ~18% vs A100 80GB for identical workloads.
   - Observed host OOM-like behavior inside the allocator (growth of slab fragmentation).
   - Mitigation: prefer per-worker soft caps or lightweight slab compaction during low-load windows.

4) Multi-tenant noise fingerprint (small batch, high interarrival jitter):
   - Some SKUs showed 'micro-jitter' correlated with noisy co-tenants: periodic small headroom drops aligned with other jobs' memcpy bursts. H100 had slightly more sensitivity to these bursts.
   - Using NIC-level RSS smoothing and increasing small-batch prefetch reduced observable p95 jitter by ~8%.

Representative numbers (aggregated, median across runs):
- A100 80GB (driver 525, CUDA11.8): steady decode throughput: 48 tokens/s; p50 18ms/token; p99 70ms/token; jitter (p99/p50)=3.9
- H100 80GB (driver 535, CUDA12.2): steady decode throughput: 60 tokens/s; p50 12ms/token; p99 96ms/token (with spikes); jitter (p99/p50)=8.0
- H100 80GB (driver 525, CUDA11.8): steady decode throughput: 58 tokens/s; p50 13ms/token; p99 28ms/token; jitter (p99/p50)=2.2
- L40S 48GB (driver 535, CUDA12.2): steady decode throughput: 42 tokens/s first 10m then drifting to 37 tokens/s after 45m; p50 22ms; p99 85ms (thermal-amplified)

Notes on reproducibility and noise:
- The H100+535.x tail events were reproducible in the same cloud region and on multiple instances, but only for specific prefill length windows and not for very short prompts. This suggests a DMA or NVLink-related scheduling interference that the driver introduced.
- Power and thermal effects on L40S can be heavily environment-dependent; replicate with identical instance family and host region when validating.
- Small differences in host kernel versions (Linux 5.10 vs 5.15) changed interrupt aggregation heuristics; include host kernel as a dimension for future runs.

Implications for runtime/serving strategies:
- Admission-time probing: implement a 60s micro-probe that runs a 2-request decode with synthetic context lengths representative of customer workloads. Record p50/p99 and p99/p50 ratio. Use this to label nodes and adjust routing.
- Automatic fallback: if a node exhibits sporadic high tail jitter, offer automatic routing to alternate SKUs or force isolated tenancy for that work.
- Model placement: prefer H100 for sustained high-throughput long-context work but gate H100 nodes on driver QC; otherwise A100 is safer for general-purpose low-variance serving.
- KV-cache placement heuristics: detect memory fragmentation signals and proactively compact or redistribute KV shards before allocation exhaustion.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Confirm root cause of H100+535.x spikes with vendor driver trace tools (NVIDIA Nsight/ CUPTI traces) and escalate to vendor if confirmed.
- Repeat L40S thermal runs with host telemetry (PDU-level) to decouple cloud host cooling variance.
- Add host kernel and network driver dims to experiment matrix and run controlled A/B tests.
- Explore microkernel patches on our runtime to reduce kernel launch fanout sensitivity seen in eBPF traces.

Immediate action items (short):

Appendix (quick checklist for rerun):
- Use identical container image hash (sha256:abc123def) for kernel code path consistency.
- Capture: dmesg, nvidia-smi sample logs (1s), runtime kernel launch histogram, eBPF attach trace around kernel launches, host cpu steal%, and NVLink error counters.
- Run at least 3 independent multi-hour runs to validate drift behaviors.
